extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and advanced graduate students interested in axiomatic/structural approaches to mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing mathematical work according to Bourbaki/Dieudonné structuralist standards: emphasis on identifying structures, stating axioms, achieving the right level of generality, and producing reusable, architecture‑aware theory. Useful for reviewing or writing research papers that aim to be part of the axiomatic 'architecture' of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and name the underlying structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizes that a phenomenon is an instance of a known structural pattern; explicitly names the relevant structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work should 'identify the underlying structure' and 'name the relevant structure explicitly' so readers can see how the result fits into the architecture (e.g., treat an example as an instance of a group, ring, topological space, etc.). This helps locate the result and facilitates reuse. Anti-pattern: treating specific examples as primary without relating them to a general structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: State definitions axiomatically and introduce minimal axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture the essence of concepts in minimal, explicit axioms rather than dependent or historical constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions should be given axiomatically ('states definitions axiomatically', 'introduce minimal axioms sufficient for the result'), so proofs can be read and checked from axioms alone. Prefer minimal sets of hypotheses; remove accidental or historical baggage when a cleaner axiomatic version exists. Scoring note: stronger when fewer, clearer axioms suffice to derive the conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove at the appropriate (ideally maximal) level of generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove results for the widest class of structures for which they hold, then specialize; avoid unnecessarily narrow statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bourbaki urges to 'maximally generalize'—show a theorem holds across a broad class (e.g., for all objects satisfying the axioms) and only then derive corollaries for special cases. But also avoid being so abstract that the result loses applicability ('neither too narrow nor too abstract'). Scoring should reward general theorems that retain meaningful content and applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structural arguments; avoid ad-hoc constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer conceptual, structure-based proofs over clever, example-specific computations or constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include 'computational virtuosity without structural insight' and 'ad-hoc construction.' A good proof is one that reveals why the result follows from the axioms and can be adapted to other instantiations of the same structure. Reusable conceptual proofs score higher than isolated clever tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure proofs are structure-preserving and do not import unnecessary structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use only structure-preserving operations (homomorphisms, continuous maps, etc.) and avoid relying on features not in the axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bourbaki emphasizes that a proof should 'use only structure-preserving operations' and 'avoid importing structure not needed for the result.' This ensures the argument is valid for all models of the axioms. Scoring: penalize proofs that rely on accidental or extra structure absent from the stated axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make proofs checkable from the axioms alone
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should be verifiable by a reader who knows only the axioms, not the author's intended interpretation or motivating intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The axiomatic method 'provides clarity and rigor'—readers should be able to follow and validate the reasoning starting from the stated axioms. Avoid appeals to unformalized intuition or domain‑specific heuristics that are not derivable from axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect results to the larger architectural hierarchy of structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Locate the result within the hierarchy (mother structures, multiple structures, theories properly particular) and explain links to adjacent structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bourbaki's program is to 'connect to the larger architecture'—authors should state how a theorem relates to algebraic/order/topological structures or combinations thereof. Good papers show how their conclusions interact with or specialize to other parts of the architecture, facilitating transfer and synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce tools and lemmas usable in adjacent areas (enable transfer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorems and lemmas should be formulated and proved so they can be reused in other contexts that instantiate the same structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'good lemma is one that other subjects will reuse.' Evaluate whether intermediate results are stated at the right level (axiomatic, general) and are likely to transfer to other instantiations; reward portability and modularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid privileging examples, historical formulations, or domain-specific schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat specific examples as primary, cling to historical formulations when a cleaner axiomatic version exists, or create tools usable only within a local/national school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns listed: 'specific examples treated as primary,' 'reverence for historical formulation when a cleaner axiomatic version exists,' and 'national/local schools that develop tools usable only within themselves.' Prefer formulations that are broadly comprehensible and adoptable across the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow Bourbakist organizational conventions (definitions → lemmas → theorems → corollaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present work in a clear axiomatic order: state definitions before theorems, prove lemmas that build to the main theorem, and give corollaries/specializations afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even opponents of Bourbaki have absorbed conventions: 'state its definitions before its theorems' and use the 'organizational template' definitions → lemmas → main theorem → corollaries. This ordering is part of readability and should be used unless a compelling alternative presentation aids understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance abstraction with problem-solving traditions (recognize scope of Bourbaki criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that Bourbaki criteria form one cluster of desirable qualities (theory-building); other clusters (problem-solving, example-driven insights) have their own valid standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critique from Arnold, Erdős, and others shows Bourbaki's standards are not universal. When evaluating work, consider whether the paper's goals are theory-building (where Bourbaki standards apply strongly) versus problem-solving or computational/explicit construction (where other criteria matter). A complete rubric should combine clusters.
